newsitem.title: SPAIN: Gonzalez not seeking re-election as party head.
newsitem.headline: Gonzalez not seeking re-election as party head.

text.p: Former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, who led Spain for 13 years, stunned supporters on Friday, announcing he would not seek re-election as the head of the Socialist Party.
"I've been at the head of the Socialist party for more than 20 years....please replace me...to open a new stage", Gonzalez told party delegates in a speech that left them in shocked silence.
Gonzalez's re-election as leader of the Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) had been seen as a mere formality at a three-day party congress which opened on Friday.
But all that changed when Gonzalez took the stage for his opening speech.
"I will continue to be available to serve this party but you should now hear that it will not be as secretary general of the party," he told more than a thousand delegates.

The 55-year-old Gonzalez gave no clear signal who he wanted to succeed him and his announcement opened the way for a leadership battle to determine who will carry the Socialist banner into the next general elections scheduled for the year 2000.
Delegates mentioned NATO Secretary General Javier Solana, a former Spanish foreign minister, and Barcelona mayor Pasqual Maragall as potential candidates.
Others speculated that Gonzalez himself could be coaxed into changing his mind and standing for re-election.
Gonzalez was 40 when his party swept to power in 1982 on a surge of popular support for his plan to rebuild the country after almost 40 years of dictatorship under General Francisco Franco.
Gonzalez was prime minister for 13 years until last year when he lost a general election to Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's conservative Popular Party.

His defeat was blamed largely on a number of corruption scandals involving the Socialists and accusations that the former government was involved in setting up undercover squads to combat the separatist violence of the Basque guerrilla group ETA.
Since then, Gonzalez has frequently spoken of being tired of public life and pushed his party to overhaul itself.

"Everyone thought it could happen but we never thought he would really do it. We thought he might say this is the last time. You could see on the faces of the executive committee that even they didn't know it was coming," Felix Dillana, a delegate from the Extremadura region told Reuters.
